start: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied
context: Mill's answer to critics who called utilitarianism a 'philosophy for pigs'. Not all pleasures are equal: the pleasures of thought and feeling are worth more.
prompt: Which of your pleasures are 'higher', and which are just easy?

start: Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so.
context: Mill learned this from his own depression at twenty. Happiness, he concluded, comes most surely when we aim at something else.
prompt: What could you care about today so much that you forget to check if you're happy?

start: If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion
context: Mill's classic defence of free expression. A lone dissenter may be right, and even if wrong, their challenge keeps the truth alive.
prompt: Whose minority opinion deserves a fairer hearing from you?

start: The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals
context: The founding principle of utilitarianism, developed by Jeremy Bentham and refined by Mill: judge actions by how much happiness and suffering they bring.
prompt: Whose happiness will your choices touch today?

start: When people who are tolerably fortunate in their outward lot
context: Mill's diagnosis of why comfortable lives can feel empty: selfishness narrows life until little in it seems worth having.
prompt: Who, beyond yourself, could you care more about?

start: He who knows only his own side of the case
context: To hold an opinion well, you must understand the best arguments against it.
prompt: Can you state the strongest case against a view you hold?

start: Those only are happy (I thought) who have their minds fixed on some object other than their own happiness
context: Mill's own recipe after his crisis: devote yourself to others, to improving the world, or to an art for its own sake, and happiness arrives on the way.
prompt: What could you fix your mind on that is bigger than your own happiness?

start: Human nature is not a machine to be built after a model
context: A plea for individuality: people are not machines to be standardised but trees that need room to grow in their own direction.
prompt: In which direction does your tree want to grow?

start: Next to selfishness, the principal cause which makes life unsatisfactory
context: A cultivated mind, Mill insists, doesn't need to be a philosopher's: just one that has been opened to learning and finds endless interest in the world.
prompt: What have you become curious about lately?

start: He who lets the world, or his own portion of it, choose his plan of life for him
context: Copying the life others choose for us takes only imitation. Choosing for ourselves uses everything we've got.
prompt: Which part of your life plan did you choose, and which did you inherit?

start: Capacity for the nobler feelings is in most natures a very tender plant
context: Our finer capacities don't die only from hostility; they wither from neglect.
prompt: Which of your finer capacities needs some nourishment?

start: The only freedom which deserves the name
context: Mill's definition of liberty: living your own way, as long as you don't stop others from living theirs.
prompt: Are you pursuing your own good in your own way?

start: Suppose that all your objects in life were realized
context: The question that triggered Mill's breakdown. He had been raised to reform the world, and realised that achieving it all would not make him happy.
prompt: If all your goals came true tomorrow, would it be enough?

start: The main constituents of a satisfied life appear to be two
context: Calm and stimulation: Mill thought most people need some balance of both to be content.
prompt: Does your life need more tranquillity, or more excitement, right now?

start: Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.
context: Where our choices affect only ourselves, Mill argues, they are ours alone to make.
prompt: Which decision about yourself are you letting others make?

start: All the grand sources, in short, of human suffering
context: Mill's hope: poverty, disease and much misfortune are not fate. Most suffering can be reduced by human effort, slowly but surely.
prompt: What suffering near you could your care and effort reduce?

start: From this moment my burden grew lighter.
context: Mill describes the moment his depression began to lift: reading a moving story, he cried, and realised he could still feel.
prompt: When did you last feel something deeply, and what did it tell you?

start: the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised
context: Mill's 'harm principle', one of the most influential ideas in modern thought: freedom ends only where harm to others begins.
prompt: Where are you trying to control what isn't harming anyone?

start: the happiness which forms the utilitarian standard of what is right in conduct
context: Utilitarianism counts everyone's happiness equally, your own included but no more than anyone else's.
prompt: How would you decide if your own happiness counted no more than another's?

start: A person whose desires and impulses are his own
context: Character, for Mill, means desires that are genuinely your own, developed by your own reflection.
prompt: Which of your desires are truly your own?

start: In them I seemed to draw from a source of inward joy
end: shared in by all human beings
context: Wordsworth's poems helped heal Mill. In them he found a joy that excluded no one.
prompt: What gives you a joy that anyone could share?

start: A person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction
end: accountable to them for the injury.
context: Doing nothing is also a choice, and it can harm others too.
prompt: Where is your inaction affecting someone?

start: Few human creatures would consent to be changed into any of the lower animals
context: Mill's argument for higher pleasures: almost nobody would trade a human life for an animal's, however comfortable.
prompt: What makes your life worth more to you than comfort?

start: the dictum that truth always triumphs over persecution
context: It's comforting to believe truth always wins. Mill warns that history says otherwise: it needs defending.
prompt: Which truth could use your defending?

start: its most appropriate appellation is a sense of dignity
context: Why would anyone prefer a harder, nobler life? Mill's answer: a sense of dignity that every human being has in some form.
prompt: What would you never do because of your own sense of dignity?

start: however true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed
context: Even true beliefs go stale when they're never questioned. Discussion keeps them alive.
prompt: Which of your beliefs have you not examined in a long time?

start: The maintenance of a due balance among the faculties
context: After his crisis, Mill decided that reason alone was not enough; feelings needed cultivating too, through poetry, art and nature.
prompt: Which side of you, thinking or feeling, needs more attention?

start: All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility.
context: Shutting down a conversation assumes we cannot be wrong.
prompt: Which conversation have you shut down because you were sure?

start: The internal sanction of duty, whatever our standard of duty may be
context: Beyond laws and reputation, our strongest guard is conscience: the inner discomfort we feel when we fall short.
prompt: What is your conscience telling you at the moment?

start: the habit of analysis has a tendency to wear away the feelings
context: Mill, trained from childhood as a reasoning machine, discovered that constant analysis can dry up feeling unless balanced by other habits.
prompt: What are you over-analysing that might simply need feeling?
